mainEntity.name: How many dental implants do I need for a bridge?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a standard implant-supported bridge, two implant posts are typically used — one at each end of the gap — to support the full restoration, including the suspended middle teeth known as pontics. In cases where a longer span of missing teeth is being replaced, additional implants may be incorporated to provide greater structural support. The precise number required will be determined during your clinical assessment, including a review of your bone density and the extent of tooth loss.

mainEntity.name: Is an implant bridge as strong as individual implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: An implant bridge can provide a strong and stable restoration and is designed to withstand normal biting forces. However, individual implants each have their own independent anchorage into the jawbone, which some clinicians consider to offer greater long-term structural resilience. The strength of either restoration is also influenced by factors such as bone quality, the materials used, and how well oral hygiene is maintained. Your dental team will discuss which option offers the most appropriate outcome for your specific needs.

mainEntity.name: How long do dental implants and implant bridges typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implants are designed as a long-term tooth replacement solution. With good oral hygiene and regular professional maintenance, many implants remain functional for a decade or more. The crown or bridge restoration placed on top of the implant may require replacement over time due to normal wear. It is not possible to provide a guaranteed lifespan, as outcomes vary depending on individual oral health, habits, and ongoing care. Your dentist will advise on what is realistic based on your circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Can I have an implant if I have already experienced bone loss?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bone loss following tooth loss is common and does not automatically rule out dental implants. In some cases, bone grafting procedures may be recommended to rebuild sufficient volume to support implant placement. The extent of bone loss and whether grafting may be appropriate will be assessed using dental imaging. This process adds time to the overall treatment journey but can make implant treatment viable for patients who might otherwise not qualify. A clinical consultation is the only way to determine whether this pathway is suitable for you.

Implant placement is carried out under local anaesthesia, meaning the area is numbed during the procedure itself. Some discomfort, swelling, and sensitivity in the days following surgery is common and generally manageable with over-the-counter pain relief as advised by your dental team. The level of post-operative discomfort varies between individuals. If you experience significant or prolonged pain following implant surgery, it is important to contact your dental practice promptly, as this may warrant clinical review.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference in cost between an implant bridge and individual implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cost will vary depending on the number of implants placed, the materials selected, the complexity of the treatment, and whether any preparatory work such as bone grafting or gum treatment is required. An implant bridge typically involves fewer implant posts than replacing each tooth individually, which may affect the overall cost. However, a detailed treatment plan and cost breakdown should be provided following your clinical consultation, allowing you to make a fully informed decision. It is advisable to discuss all associated costs, including ongoing maintenance, before committing to treatment.
